column1: # Every expectation below was derived BY HAND from the authoritative
# Pure ASCII on purpose, so no encoding can corrupt it.
# The cases marked [HAZARD] specifically guard the bridge-character trick:
# e.g. after 'sh' folds to a bridge char, the trailing "ui" must NOT be
# re-matched by the ui rule. If the bridge trick is broken, these fail.
# CORRECTIONS made after the first self-test run (4 of my expectations
# were wrong, the converter was right):
#   wen -> wf   (wen = w + en,  NOT w + un)
#   wei -> wz   (wei = w + ei,  NOT w + ui)
#   hun -> hp   (I had duplicated hen's expectation by mistake)
#   ou  -> ou   (see the zero-initial note below)
# ZERO-INITIAL SYLLABLES - the real rule, verified against the algebra:
#   Each zero-initial syllable keeps its PLAIN spelling, and ADDITIONALLY
#   gets an 'o'-prefixed variant (because 'derive' adds, it does not
#   replace). The o-prefixed variant is  o + <the final's key>:
#     ou : ou  or ob     <-- note the plain form stays "ou"
#   The asymmetry on "ou" happens because the rule form is
#   which needs at least one character BEFORE "ou". The bare 2-char
#   spelling "ou" therefore never matches, and survives untouched.
#   This is worth testing against iOS native - see the keylist.
# --- zero-initial family (plain form; o-prefixed form also accepted) ---
